0.title: The Rest We Were Made For
0.essay:
The alarm goes, and before your feet touch the floor you have checked your messages. The day is a list, and the list is longer than the day. You eat standing up. In the evening you are exhausted, yet when you finally sit down you feel you ought to be doing something. If you know that feeling, this study is for you.

Tired in body, restless in heart

Ask people how they are, and many will say, “Busy.” Sometimes they say it with a sigh, and sometimes with a little pride. Our calendars are full, our phones never fall silent, and many of us carry a low hum of guilt whenever we stop. We are tired, but it is not only our bodies that are tired. Something in us cannot settle.

The Bible knows this condition well. It speaks of people who “rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil” (Psalm 127:2). It also speaks of a God who gives rest, and of a Saviour who says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Where we are going

This study does not offer a time-management system, and it is not written to make busy people feel guilty for being busy. It begins by naming the hurried, always-on life honestly. Then it looks underneath, at what drives us. It shows that our limits are a gift from a God who never tires, and it looks at Jesus, the most purposeful and least hurried person who ever lived. It walks with Elijah when he was spent, and it ends with practical wisdom for days, weeks and years.

Several other studies touch this ground, and this one does not repeat them. Christian at Work has a chapter on rest and the Sabbath, Worship & the Lord’s Day explains the Lord’s Day in full, and Technology & the Christian Mind looks closely at our phones. If you are weighed down by low mood rather than tiredness, the study Depression & the Christian is written for you.

The chapters

Always On; What Drives the Hurry; Dust, Sleep and the Seventh Day; The Unhurried Saviour; Under the Broom Tree; and Rhythms of Grace.

For reflection

When did you last stop completely, without feeling guilty about it? If someone asked you honestly why you are so busy, what would you say?

1.title: Always On
1.essay:
It does not usually feel like a problem. It feels like life. There is work to do, children to collect, messages to answer, a church rota to fill, a parent to visit. Every piece of it is good. And yet the whole of it can leave you running from one thing to the next without ever quite arriving.

The shape of a hurried life

Hurry has a recognisable shape. You walk faster than you need to. You choose the shortest queue and still feel impatient in it. You read half an email and reply to the half you read. You eat at your desk, or in the car, or not at all. Conversations become transactions: you are listening, but part of you is already in the next meeting. Even good things, like a meal with friends or an evening with your family, are slotted into gaps and watched with one eye on the clock.

Then there is the phone. It goes everywhere, to the table, to the bathroom, to bed. It means that work, news and other people’s lives can reach you at any hour. There is no longer a moment when the day is simply over. Many people check it within minutes of waking and minutes before sleep. The result is a mind that is never quite off duty.

Tired in a new way

This produces a particular kind of tiredness. Your body may be weary, but your mind will not stop. You lie down, and the list begins: the thing you forgot, the email you must send, the conversation tomorrow. The Teacher in Ecclesiastes described it three thousand years ago: “For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest” (Ecclesiastes 2:23).

The psalmist saw people rushing about and said, “Surely for nothing they are in turmoil” (Psalm 39:6). Not every busy life is for nothing. But it is possible to be very busy and to gain very little, to sow much and harvest little, as the prophet Haggai told the people of his day (Haggai 1:6).

Guilty when resting

One of the strangest marks of this condition is guilt when we stop. You sit down on a Saturday afternoon with a book, and a voice says, “You should be doing something useful.” You take a holiday and check your work email on the first morning, just in case. You feel you must explain to others, and to yourself, why you were not productive. Rest has become something you must earn, and you never feel you have quite earned it.

The opposite can happen too. Some people are so drained that when they stop they cannot rest at all. They scroll, or watch one more episode, or drift without being refreshed. They are not working, but they are not resting either. Their stillness is only a pause in the noise.

Not every kind of busy is the same

We must be careful here. Some seasons are simply full, and Scripture does not scold people for them. Parents of small children, those caring for a sick husband or wife or an ageing parent, those working two jobs to pay the rent, students at exam time, farmers at harvest: these are not people with disordered hearts. They are people carrying real loads, and they need help, not a lecture. Much of this study is for them too, but they should hear first that God sees them, and that “he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14).

Nor is this study a defence of idleness. The Bible warns plainly against laziness: “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber” (Proverbs 6:10–11). Work is good, as the study Christian at Work shows. The problem this study addresses is not work. It is the driven, anxious, never-enough way of living that can grip people who work very hard indeed.

Martha’s question

Luke tells of a home in Bethany where Jesus was a guest. Martha, the host, was busy with all the preparation, and finally she came to Jesus and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?” (Luke 10:40). Many of us know that tone of voice. It is the voice of someone doing good things and feeling that the whole weight rests on her. We will come back to Jesus’ answer later. For now it is enough to notice that he heard her, and that he did not leave her as she was.

An example

A man in his forties runs a small building firm. He starts at six, answers customers’ messages until ten at night and works most Saturdays. He tells himself it is for his family. One Sunday his twelve-year-old daughter asks him why he is always looking at his phone. He has no good answer. On the drive home from church he realises he cannot remember the last time he sat with her without one ear on his work.

For reflection

Which parts of the hurried life described here do you recognise in yourself? When do you feel most guilty for resting? Is your busyness mostly a season you are passing through, or a way of life you have chosen? What might the people closest to you say about how you spend your time?

2.title: What Drives the Hurry
2.essay:
Busyness is often a symptom. Our calendars are like a window into our hearts. When we cannot stop, it is worth asking why. Usually, without realising it, we are asking our activity to give us something that only God can give.

Unless the LORD builds

Psalm 127 begins, “Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain” (Psalm 127:1). The psalm does not tell us to stop building or stop keeping watch. It tells us that our effort is not what holds the world together. When we forget that, work turns into “the bread of anxious toil” (Psalm 127:2): labour eaten with worry, as if everything depended on us.

Underneath the anxious toil there are usually some quieter beliefs. Here are five of the most common.

“I am what I produce”

For many of us, worth is measured by output. A good day is a productive day, and a good person is a useful one. So when we stop, we feel we have stopped being worth anything. Retirement, illness or redundancy can feel like a kind of death, because the thing that told us who we were has gone.

Ecclesiastes describes a man who works alone with “no end to all his toil”, and who never stops to ask, “For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?” (Ecclesiastes 4:8). Jesus warned that “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15), and the same is true of achievements. You are not your output. You are a creature made by God, and, if you trust Christ, a child loved by him before you have done anything at all.

“If I stop, it will fall apart”

Some busyness is driven by fear. If I do not answer that message tonight, I might lose the client. If I do not check everything twice, something will go wrong. If I slow down, I will fall behind. Fear keeps the engine running long after the body has asked it to stop. Jesus asks a gentle question: “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” (Matthew 6:27). Worry promises safety but cannot deliver it.

“I must stay in control”

Being busy can feel like being in charge. While we are working, we are managing outcomes. Rest means letting go, and letting go feels dangerous. James speaks to people making confident plans: “yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:14–15). The constant hurry is sometimes an attempt to hold a world that was never ours to hold.

“I cannot say no”

Many of us are busy because we cannot bear to disappoint anyone. Every request feels like a test of whether we are a good friend, a good church member, a good employee. So we say yes, and then yes again, and our lives fill with other people’s expectations. Paul’s question cuts through this: “For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God?” (Galatians 1:10). Saying yes to everyone is not the same as loving everyone. The study The Fear of Man explores this snare in depth.

“I do not want to be quiet”

This one is harder to admit. Noise and activity can be a way of not feeling. If I stop, I might notice that I am sad, or lonely, or afraid, or far from God. The French thinker Blaise Pascal observed that much of human unhappiness comes from our inability to sit quietly in a room. Distraction numbs us.

Isaiah spoke to Judah when they were rushing to Egypt for help against Assyria. God said, “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength” (Isaiah 30:15). But a sad line follows: “But you were unwilling.” They preferred horses: “We will flee upon horses” (Isaiah 30:16). Speed felt safer than stillness. We can be just the same.

A restless heart

Behind all five lies something deeper. Augustine of Hippo wrote, at the start of his Confessions, that God has made us for himself and that our hearts are restless until they rest in him. Busyness is often the outward form of that restlessness. We are looking for rest in the right direction but in the wrong place: in success, safety, control, approval or noise. None of them can bear the weight. Only God can.

An example

A woman in her fifties is on four church rotas, leads a toddler group and cares for her grandchildren twice a week. Everyone calls her a saint. When her pastor asks how she is, she bursts into tears. Later, talking it through, she sees that she has never felt loved unless she was useful. She has been serving partly to earn a welcome that God had already given her.

For reflection

Which of the five beliefs, about worth, fear, control, approval or silence, drives you most? What do you think would happen if you stopped for a whole day? Where are you looking for a rest that only God can give? Pray Psalm 127:1–2 slowly, and ask God to show you what you are building without him.

3.title: Dust, Sleep and the Seventh Day
3.essay:
There is only one being in the universe who never needs to stop. Everything else, from the stars to the sparrows to you, is limited, dependent and made. This is not bad news. It is the beginning of rest.

The God who never tires

“Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4). Isaiah asks the weary exiles, “Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable” (Isaiah 40:28).

Think what that means. While you sleep, God is awake. He holds the galaxies in their courses and numbers the hairs on your head, and he is never stretched, never behind, never running on empty. The Son, Paul tells us, “is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). The world does not need you to hold it together. It already has someone doing that, and he is very good at it.

Creatures, not machines

We, by contrast, are dust. “For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). God made us with bodies that need food, water and sleep every single day. We can be in one place at a time and do one thing well at a time. These limits are not the result of sin. Adam in the garden, before the fall, needed to eat and was given work to do in one place (Genesis 2:15–16). God looked at a world full of limited creatures and called it “very good” (Genesis 1:31).

So our limits are not a failure to be ashamed of. They are part of the goodness of being made. To live within them is to accept that I am a creature and that God is God. Much of our exhaustion comes from quietly refusing that, and trying to live as if we were tireless and indispensable.

Evening, then morning

Genesis counts the days in a striking way: “And there was evening and there was morning, the first day” (Genesis 1:5). In the Bible’s reckoning the day begins at evening. Many have noticed what that suggests for us. Our day does not begin when we get up and start work. It begins as we lie down. We sleep, and God keeps working. We wake up into a day that he has already begun.

God rested

Then comes the seventh day. “And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done” (Genesis 2:2). God was not tired. The word means he ceased. His work was complete, and he stopped to enjoy what he had made. “So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy” (Genesis 2:3).

Notice that rest is woven into the world before sin enters it. Rest is not a repair kit for a broken creation. It belongs to creation as God designed it. And notice that the seventh day, unlike the six before it, has no closing words about evening and morning. Many readers have seen in this a hint that God’s rest is not simply a day that passes, but a rest he means to share with his people. Hebrews will take up that thought, and the next chapter follows it to Christ.

He gives to his beloved sleep

“It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Sleep is a gift, given to people God loves. It is also a nightly lesson in trust. Every evening you lay down your tools, close your eyes and become, for a few hours, completely helpless. The world goes on without you. Your work waits. And God keeps you.

David knew this when his own son Absalom had taken the throne and David was running for his life. The heading of Psalm 3 tells us so. Yet he wrote, “I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me” (Psalm 3:5). The next psalm ends, “In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). Sleep in that setting is not laziness. It is faith with its eyes closed.

This does not mean that everyone who struggles to sleep lacks faith. Insomnia has many causes, physical and emotional, and some need a doctor’s help. But it does mean that going to bed on time can be an act of worship, a way of saying, “You are God, and I am not.”

Strength for the faint

Isaiah’s great chapter goes on: “He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength. Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted; but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:29–31). Even the strongest run out. The difference is not between those who get tired and those who do not, but between those who run on their own strength and those who wait on the Lord.

An example

A university student is proud of how little he sleeps. He works until three, wakes at eight and lives on coffee. By the second term he is ill, irritable and falling behind. A chaplain reads Psalm 127 with him and asks whether he thinks God can run the world for seven hours without his help. He laughs, but the question stays with him. He starts going to bed before midnight, praying Psalm 4:8 as he turns out the light.

For reflection

Which of your limits do you find hardest to accept? How does it change things to know that your day begins as you lie down? Do you think of sleep as a waste of time or as a gift? What would it mean for you to “wait for the LORD” this week?

4.title: The Unhurried Saviour
4.essay:
Jesus was given the greatest work in history and about three years of public ministry in which to do it. Crowds pressed on him, needs were endless, and enemies watched his every move. Yet you never see him in a hurry. And at the end he could say that his work was done.

Never hurried, never idle

Jesus worked hard. There were days when “many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat” (Mark 6:31). He grew tired, and sat down by a well, “wearied as he was from his journey” (John 4:6). He slept so deeply in a boat that a storm did not wake him: “he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion” (Mark 4:38). The Son of God took a real body that needed rest. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). He knows what it is to be exhausted.

Yet he was never driven. On the way to the house of Jairus, whose daughter was dying, a woman touched his cloak in the crowd. Jesus stopped. “Who touched my garments?” (Mark 5:30). The disciples thought the question absurd. But Jesus took time to look for her, to hear “the whole truth” and to call her “Daughter” (Mark 5:33–34). He went on to raise Jairus’ daughter, but he was never so hurried that a person became an interruption.

He withdrew

Mark records a day in Capernaum crowded with healing. Then: “And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed” (Mark 1:35). The disciples hunted him down and said, “Everyone is looking for you” (Mark 1:37). Jesus answered, “Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out” (Mark 1:38).

There were still sick people in Capernaum, and everyone wanted him. But Jesus knew what his Father had sent him to do, and he had heard it again in the dark that morning. Prayer did not make him busier. It made him clear. Luke says this was his habit: “But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray” (Luke 5:16).

He did the same for his friends. When the apostles came back from their mission, worn out, he said, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while” (Mark 6:31). The plan did not work out. The crowd ran ahead, and when Jesus saw them, “he had compassion on them” (Mark 6:34). Rest mattered to him, but love mattered more. He was neither a slave to the crowd nor a slave to his schedule.

One thing is necessary

Back in Bethany, Martha had asked, “Lord, do you not care?” Jesus answered gently, repeating her name: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:41–42).

Jesus did not scold Martha for cooking. He named what was going on inside her: anxious, troubled, pulled apart by many things. And he pointed her to the one thing, himself. Martha was serving Jesus so busily that she was missing Jesus.

The work that was finished

On the night before he died, Jesus prayed, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). He had not healed every sick person in Israel or preached in every town. Yet he had done everything the Father gave him. That is the measure of a faithful life: not every need met, but the given work done.

And then he did the one work none of us could ever do. On the cross he bore the sins of his people, and he cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30). Hebrews pictures the priests of Israel standing day after day, because their work was never done. But “when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). He sat down. The work that saves us is complete. There is nothing left for us to add.

Here is the deepest answer to our restlessness. Much of our hurry is a hidden attempt to prove that we are worth something. The gospel says the proving has been done, by someone else, once for all.

Come to me

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

A yoke joined two oxen to share a load. Jesus does not invite us to come and do nothing. He invites us to come and work alongside him. The yoke is easy because of who is in the other half of it: one who is “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The rest he offers is not first a day off. It is a person. It is to be known, loved and accepted by him, and then to work from that place instead of towards it.

Rest as trust

Hebrews puts it plainly: “For we who have believed enter that rest” (Hebrews 4:3). “So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his” (Hebrews 4:9–10). God’s seventh-day rest, the rest he meant to share, is entered by faith in Christ, now in part and fully in glory. Hebrews even says, “Let us therefore strive to enter that rest” (Hebrews 4:11). The hardest work for a driven heart is to stop striving and trust.

An example

A primary school teacher reads Luke 10 and sees herself in Martha. She decides to begin each school day with ten minutes of sitting still with an open Bible before she opens her laptop. She notices that she is kinder to the children by eleven o’clock, and that she no longer feels that the whole school depends on her.

For reflection

Which moment in Jesus’ life speaks most to your hurry? What might Jesus say to you if he repeated your name, as he did Martha’s? How does it help you that Christ “sat down” when his work was done? What would it mean for you to work from his acceptance instead of towards it?

5.title: Under the Broom Tree
5.essay:
Sometimes tiredness becomes something more. The tank does not just run low; it runs dry. People call it burnout. The Bible does not use the word, but it tells the story of a great prophet who reached the end of himself, and of how gently God met him there.

After the mountain top

Elijah had just had the greatest day of his ministry. On Mount Carmel, fire fell from heaven, the people cried that the LORD is God, and the prophets of Baal were defeated. Then “the hand of the LORD was on Elijah, and he gathered up his garment and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel” (1 Kings 18:46), a run of many miles.

Then Queen Jezebel sent a single message threatening his life. “Then he was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life” (1 Kings 19:3). He went into the wilderness and sat under a broom tree. “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers” (1 Kings 19:4).

Notice the pattern. Burnout often comes after a long stretch of intense effort and little rest, and then one more blow that is one too many. The person who seemed strongest is suddenly empty.

Sleep and bread first

What did God do? He did not rebuke him. “And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, ‘Arise and eat’” (1 Kings 19:5). Elijah ate, drank and slept again. Then the angel came a second time: “Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7).

God knows when the journey is too great for us. His first answer to a worn-out servant was not a sermon but sleep, food and a touch. The body matters to God. Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is to eat a proper meal and go to bed.

A truer picture

Only after that did God speak to Elijah’s heart. At Horeb he asked, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (1 Kings 19:9). Elijah replied, “I, even I only, am left” (1 Kings 19:10). Exhaustion had shrunk his world. He felt that everything depended on him and that he had failed. God came to him not in wind, earthquake or fire but in “the sound of a low whisper” (1 Kings 19:12), and he corrected the picture: “Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal” (1 Kings 19:18).

The study Depression & the Christian looks at this conversation more fully. Here notice one thing: burnout often comes with the belief that I am indispensable. God’s cure was to show Elijah that he was not alone and never had been. The work was God’s, and God had many servants.

Shared loads

God also gave Elijah a companion. He told him to anoint Elisha, and Elisha “arose and went after Elijah and assisted him” (1 Kings 19:21). Elijah did not go back to carrying everything alone.

Moses learned the same lesson. He sat judging the people from morning to evening until his father-in-law Jethro said, “What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone” (Exodus 18:17–18). Moses listened, and shared the work, as the apostles later did (Acts 6:1–4). Asking for help is not failure. It is how God designed his people to work.

Warning signs

Burnout usually builds slowly, and it is easy to miss in yourself. Watch for these signs:

Exhaustion that rest no longer fixes. A weekend or even a holiday makes little difference. Cynicism and distance. You stop caring about people you used to care about, and you feel numb or bitter about your work or ministry. A sense of futility. Nothing you do seems to make any difference. A short fuse. You snap at those closest to you. Poor sleep, frequent minor illnesses, headaches or a racing heart. Leaning on props, such as more caffeine, alcohol, food or hours of scrolling, just to keep going or to switch off. Losing joy in God: prayer feels like one more task, and church like another shift.

If several of these describe you, take them seriously. They are warning lights, not signs that you are a weak Christian.

When to see a doctor

Please see your doctor if exhaustion lasts for weeks, if you cannot sleep or cannot get up, if you have chest pains, panic attacks or a racing heart, or if low mood will not lift. Burnout and depression often overlap, and some physical conditions, such as anaemia or thyroid problems, can look like simple tiredness. Seeing a doctor or a qualified counsellor is not a failure of faith, and medicine, where it is prescribed, is one of God’s good gifts. You may need time off work, and that is not shameful either.

Like Elijah, some people in the depths of exhaustion begin to wish they were dead. If you have thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust today.

The bruised reed

Matthew applies Isaiah’s prophecy to Jesus: “a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench” (Matthew 12:20). If you feel like a wick that has almost gone out, this is how Christ treats you. He shields what is barely burning.

An example

A youth worker has run three summer camps in a row, as well as his weekly groups. In September he finds he dreads every message from a parent. He cannot pray, sleeps badly and snaps at his wife. A friend persuades him to see his doctor, who signs him off for three weeks. His church leaders find two volunteers to share the load. Months later he is back, with a team instead of alone.

For reflection

Which of the warning signs do you notice in yourself, if any? Why do you think God gave Elijah sleep and food before he spoke to him? Where do you believe, like Elijah, that “I, even I only, am left”? Who could share part of your load?

6.title: Rhythms of Grace
6.essay:
The gospel does not give busy people a new list of rules to perform. It gives them rest in Christ, and then invites them into rhythms that fit creatures who are loved. What follows is wisdom, not law. Take what helps, and leave the rest without guilt.

Daily: begin and end with God

The psalmist says, “It is good to give thanks to the LORD … to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night” (Psalm 92:1–2). Consider giving God the first minutes of your day before you give them to your phone. Even a short time with Scripture and prayer can turn the day from a list into a gift.

Set a time when work stops: a time after which work email stays closed, a walk or a meal that marks the end of the working day. At night, hand the day back to God, finished and unfinished parts alike, and pray Psalm 4:8 as you turn out the light. Most adults need around seven to nine hours of sleep. Going to bed is not wasted time. It is trusting the God who “will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4).

Weekly: the Lord’s Day as a gift

From creation God gave a rhythm of six days and one. For Christians, the first day of the week, the day Christ rose, is “the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10), when the church gathers to worship. Christians hold different views on how this day relates to the Sabbath. Many godly believers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment continues as a moral law, so that Sunday is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept by rest from ordinary work and recreation for worship and mercy. Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday as the Sabbath. Others hold that the Sabbath, as a sign of the old covenant, is fulfilled in Christ, while the Lord’s Day remains the day of gathered worship.

This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who is our true rest, and Sunday is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest out of joy and wisdom, not a law with rules about work. Paul calls the Sabbath “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17), and he says of special days, “Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5). No one may bind another’s conscience. Those who keep Sunday as a Sabbath do so “in honor of the Lord” (Romans 14:6), and their careful keeping of the day is a faithful witness that deserves honour, not mockery. The study Worship & the Lord’s Day sets out the question in full.

For a tired person, this is good news. Sunday is not another task. It is a gift to receive: worship with God’s people, an unhurried meal, a walk, friends, sleep. “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). If your work means you serve on Sundays, as nurses, carers and pastors do, it is wise to keep another day each week for rest.

Yearly: seasons of rest

Israel’s year had its own rhythm. Three times a year the people went up to the great feasts (Deuteronomy 16:16), and every seventh year even the land had “a Sabbath of solemn rest” (Leviticus 25:4). God thinks in seasons. Take your holidays, and make them real holidays. Some find it helpful to set aside a day or two each year for quiet, prayer and stepping back.

Saying no

Jesus left Capernaum while people were still looking for him, because he knew what he was sent to do (Mark 1:38). You too will have to say no to good things in order to say yes to the things God has actually given you. Before you agree to something new, pause. Ask what it will push out, and whether you are saying yes from love or from fear. “Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind” (Ecclesiastes 4:6). Then let your answer be clear and kind: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). The study Knowing God’s Will offers help with choices like these.

Digital habits

“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but I will not be dominated by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12). Small habits can loosen the phone’s grip: turn off most notifications; charge the phone outside the bedroom; check email at set times, not constantly; keep meals free of screens; leave the phone behind for part of each Sunday. The study Technology & the Christian Mind explores this further.

Resting without guilt

When guilt rises as you rest, answer it with the truth. Rest is not stolen time. It is a gift: “There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God” (Ecclesiastes 2:24). You are not resting because you have earned it, but because you are a creature and a child, and your Father gives it. If the guilt is part of a wider habit of condemning yourself, the study Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation may help.

Rest for others

Some people cannot easily choose their rhythms: carers, single parents, shift workers. Churches can help them rest, with a meal, some childcare or an afternoon off for a carer. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

The rest that is coming

Every night’s sleep and every Lord’s Day points forward. One day the restlessness will end. “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on … that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!” (Revelation 14:13). In the new creation there will be no anxious toil, and no heart that cannot settle.

An example

A couple with two jobs and three children realise their family has no rhythm at all. They make small changes: phones in a basket at meals, church and a long lunch on Sundays, work email closed after eight. They keep one week each summer completely free. A year later the eldest says Sunday lunch is her favourite part of the week.

Further reading

Kevin DeYoung’s Crazy Busy is a short, honest book on busyness. Christopher Ash’s Zeal Without Burnout is written for Christian workers and full of wisdom about sleep, Sabbath and friendship.

For reflection

Which one rhythm, daily, weekly or yearly, do you most need to begin? What is one thing you need to say no to in this season? How could you receive next Sunday as a gift rather than a task? Who around you needs help to rest, and what could you do for them?
